analysis.one_liner: Required training and certification for subprime mortgage brokers and lenders, banned unfair and deceptive lending practices, and voided forced arbitration clauses in consumer contracts.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the House Financial Services Committee until the Congress ended, after the 2008 housing collapse had already shown the scale of the problem it addressed.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required anyone making or brokering subprime mortgages to pass a federal certification exam showing they understand subprime lending and predatory practices, and it would have let regulators suspend or revoke that certification. It would have banned unfair or deceptive practices in subprime lending — including pressuring appraisers to inflate home values — with civil penalties up to $10,000 per day. It would have forced lenders on high-cost mortgages to disclose all fees clearly, resolve complaints in good faith within 60 days, and made forced arbitration clauses unenforceable in consumer contracts, so wronged borrowers could go to court. It also funded community groups to educate borrowers about predatory lending. The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee in April 2007 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Home buyers and homeowners taking out subprime or high-cost mortgages would have gained the most: certified and trained loan originators, clear disclosure of every fee before signing, a good-faith review of any complaint with a 60-day freeze on collection and foreclosure during it, and civil penalties for lenders and brokers who engaged in unfair or deceptive practices or pressured appraisers. All consumers, not just mortgage borrowers, would have gained the right to take disputes to court instead of being forced into binding arbitration by fine print. Community groups would have received grants to teach borrowers how to spot predatory loans.

how_it_helps.text: It would have required anyone providing subprime lending or mortgage brokerage services to be certified by HUD as trained in subprime and predatory lending practices, with suspension and revocation for violators [S2, S3].

It would have barred unfair or deceptive acts in subprime lending and brokerage — including pressuring appraisers to inflate home values or submitting false appraisals — with civil penalties up to $10,000 per day, doubling to $20,000 for repeat violations [S3].

For high-cost mortgages, it would have required lenders to adopt best-practices plans, resolve consumer complaints in good faith within 60 days (with no foreclosure or collection action during that window), and banned fees not disclosed before the loan was signed [S3].
It would have made mandatory binding arbitration clauses unenforceable in all consumer contracts, letting consumers take disputes to court after the dispute arises [S2, S3].
It authorized $2 million a year for grants to nonprofit community development corporations to educate borrowers and community groups about predatory lending [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: Subprime mortgage lenders and brokers would have borne the cost: training and certification requirements, compliance with best-practices plans, daily civil penalties for violations, and exposure to lawsuits now that forced arbitration clauses would be unenforceable. Businesses across the consumer economy that rely on mandatory arbitration clauses would also have lost that tool. Some of the compliance cost could have been passed to borrowers through higher loan prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill would have required every person providing subprime lending or brokerage services to pass a federal certification exam and be recertified periodically, a licensing regime that could have raised the cost of serving subprime borrowers and shrunk access to credit for people with low incomes or poor credit — the very borrowers the subprime market existed to serve [S3].
The mortgage would have frozen collection and foreclosure for 60 days after any consumer complaint, even a questionable one, which lenders would bear as added delay and risk on high-cost loans [S3].

The mandatory-arbitration ban went well beyond mortgages, covering all consumer contracts — a broad change to how businesses of every kind manage disputes that its critics would call sweeping and its supporters would call the point.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to home buyers were large and the costs fell on a narrow industry: licensing exams for brokers, honest disclosures, civil penalties for fraud, and a right to take disputes to court instead of forced arbitration. An honest objection is design, not direction: the bill was written in 2007, before the housing collapse, and some rules — mandatory certification of every subprime lending professional and a 60-day freeze on foreclosures after any complaint — were broad and untested, and could have raised costs or slowed credit for exactly the risky borrowers the subprime market served. But the bill never got a hearing, so those design questions were never weighed against the foreclosures that followed.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee in April 2007 and never advanced — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and expired when the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Stephanie Tubbs Jones of Ohio introduced the bill on April 26, 2007, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services [S1, S5].

The complete action history shows only the introduction, the committee referral, and two sets of the sponsor's introductory remarks — no hearings, no committee markup, and no floor action were ever recorded [S5].
The bill died in committee when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S1, S5].
All 16 cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican signed on, and no companion Senate bill appears in the record [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Subprime mortgage lenders and brokers, and the arbitration industry, were better off: they faced no new certification requirements, disclosure rules, civil penalties, or enforceability limits on arbitration clauses, and the bill expired just as the housing crisis made those practices central to millions of foreclosures.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Mortgage lenders, brokers, and arbitration firms

for.name: Rep. Stephanie Tubbs Jones
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in April 2007 and delivered introductory remarks on it twice [S1, S5].

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Barney Frank (D-MA)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it received no action after referral and died in committee at the end of the 110th Congress [S5].

sides.party_line_note: All 16 cosponsors were Democrats and the sponsor was a Democrat; no Republican cosponsor appears in the record, and the bill never advanced far enough for a roll-call vote to show how the parties would have split [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have required federal certification and training for anyone originating or brokering subprime loans, banned unfair or deceptive practices with penalties up to $10,000 per day, and restricted undisclosed fees on high-cost mortgages. It died, so none of these constraints took effect through this bill.

The bill's Consumer Fairness Act title would have made mandatory binding arbitration clauses unenforceable across all consumer contracts, removing a large volume of disputes from private arbitration. It never became law, so the industry's role in consumer contracts was untouched.

The bill authorized $2 million a year in grants to nonprofits for teaching borrowers about predatory lending, creating a funded role for these groups in consumer education. That funding never materialized.

The bill would have penalized lenders who pressured appraisers to inflate property values, protecting independent appraisers from coercion, while exposing appraisers who knowingly submitted false appraisals to penalties. The bill died, leaving appraisal pressure unaddressed by this legislation.
